finding.question: Under current U.S. election rules, can an otherwise valid mail-in ballot postmarked before Election Day be counted if it arrives after Election Day, and how does this depend on the jurisdiction and arrival date?
finding.summary: As of October 28, 2020, an otherwise valid ballot postmarked before Election Day could be counted after Election Day in some jurisdictions, provided it arrived by the applicable deadline. For the November 3 election, California allowed receipt through November 20 and Kansas through November 6 for ballots postmarked by Election Day. Michigan generally required receipt by 8 p.m. on November 3. In North Carolina, a court-approved extension allowed qualifying ballots to arrive by 5 p.m. on November 12.

sources.title: Supreme Court Leaves NC Absentee Ballot Deadline at Nov. 12
sources.snippet: The justices, by a 5-3 vote Wednesday, refused to disturb a decision by the State Board of Elections to lengthen the period from three to nine days because of the coronavirus pandemic, pushing back the deadline to Nov. 12. The board’s decision was part of a legal settlement with a union-affiliated group....Under the Supreme Court’s order, mailed ballots postmarked on or before Election Day must be received by 5 p.m. on Nov. 12 in order to be counted.

caveats: These examples describe rules for the November 2020 election, not present-day deadlines or every jurisdiction.
Some voters, including military and overseas voters, may be subject to separate rules.

report_raw.claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
report_raw.justification: For the November 2020 election, California required officials to count otherwise valid ballots postmarked by Election Day and received within 17 days afterward. [S1] Kansas likewise accepted ballots postmarked by Election Day if received by November 6. [S2] Rules varied: Michigan generally required absentee ballots to arrive by 8 p.m. on Election Day. [S3] Thus, as a general assertion about U.S. elections, the claim is false; whether a late-arriving ballot could be counted depended on the jurisdiction and its deadline. [S1][S2][S3]
key_points: California allowed qualifying ballots to arrive up to 17 days after Election Day. [S1]
Kansas allowed qualifying ballots to arrive by November 6, three days after Election Day. [S2]
Michigan generally required receipt by 8 p.m. on Election Day. [S3]
North Carolina allowed qualifying ballots to arrive by 5 p.m. on November 12. [S4]
report_raw.counter_argument: The claim describes the general rule in Michigan, where absentee ballots had to be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day. [S3] It does not prevail as a general assertion because California and Kansas expressly allowed qualifying ballots received after Election Day to be counted. [S1][S2]
evidence_gaps: The evidence does not provide a comprehensive inventory of deadlines in every jurisdiction or separate rules for military and overseas voters.
